attachments.origin_landmark: posterior surface of the cricoid lamina (the laryngeal cartilages are not modeled as skeletal elements in this pass -- approximated via the adjacent hyoid attachment region)
attachments.insertion_landmark: muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage

actions: abducts the vocal folds, opening the rima glottidis

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: The only ABDUCTOR of the vocal folds, and therefore the only muscle that opens the airway at the glottis. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy leaves the folds unopposed in adduction and causes stridor and airway obstruction, which is why bilateral injury is an emergency while unilateral injury merely causes hoarseness.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Percutaneous EMG-guided injection, not ultrasound: two described routes -- (1) through the cricothyroid membrane in the midline, with the needle then passed posterolaterally hugging the inner surface of the cricoid cartilage around to its posterior lamina where PCA lies; or (2) a direct posterolateral approach, inserting the needle through the skin lateral to the cricoid cartilage (sometimes with the head rotated to the opposite side) and walking it onto the posterior cricoid lamina. EMG confirms placement as the patient sniffs/inspires forcefully (PCA is the only laryngeal abductor and fires with inspiration).
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Posterior to the cricoid cartilage lamina, in the retrocricoid region -- deeper and more posterior than thyroarytenoid or lateral cricoarytenoid, and technically more difficult to reach and to confirm by EMG.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: EMG activity that is phasic with inspiration (increasing on a sniff) rather than with phonation confirms PCA rather than an adductor muscle.
structures_at_risk: esophagus, immediately posterior to the cricoid lamina and PCA

the other adductor muscles via diffusion around the muscular process of the arytenoid -- the presumed mechanism of the rare bilateral abductor paralysis/stridor reported after adjacent thyroarytenoid injection, and the reason bilateral PCA injection for abductor spasmodic dysphonia is more technically demanding and less reliably effective than adductor (thyroarytenoid) injection
interarytenoid muscle, whose nerve branch is closely connected to that of PCA's horizontal compartment in nearly all specimens
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Human PCA is supplied by at least two separable nerve branches (an upper branch to a horizontal compartment, a lower branch to vertical/oblique compartments per Sihler staining), but this compartmental mapping has not been translated into a percent-along-the-muscle injection target in the literature, so no motor_endplate_zones entry is given here -- ultrasound_injection_approach is the field with real, quantifiable data for this muscle. Clinically used for abductor spasmodic dysphonia (weakening the only vocal fold abductor), posterior glottic insufficiency/synkinesis after vocal fold paresis, and -- more recently -- as a bridging or airway-preserving treatment for bilateral vocal fold paralysis with aspiration. Reported response rates/duration are lower than for thyroarytenoid injection in adductor spasmodic dysphonia, attributed in part to the technical difficulty of accurate needle placement. Guidance is by EMG, never ultrasound.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Blitzer A, Brin MF, Stewart CF, 'Botulinum toxin management of spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia): a 12-year experience in more than 900 patients', Laryngoscope 108(10):1435-1441 (1998), doi:10.1097/00005537-199810000-00003 (https://doi.org/10.1097/00005537-199810000-00003); Sanders I, Wu BL, Mu L, Biller HF, 'The innervation of the human posterior cricoarytenoid muscle: evidence for at least two neuromuscular compartments', Laryngoscope 104(7):880-884 (1994), doi:10.1288/00005537-199407000-00019 (https://doi.org/10.1288/00005537-199407000-00019) -- 15 human PCA specimens, Sihler staining; Razura DE, Merati AL, Johns MM 3rd, Santa Maria C, 'Posterior Cricoarytenoid Muscle Chemodenervation Can Improve Voice in Recalcitrant Dysphonia in Unilateral Vocal Fold Paresis With Synkinesis', J Voice (2024), doi:10.1016/j.jvoice.2024.11.007 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvoice.2024.11.007) -- percutaneous EMG-guided technique; Ata N, Ozturk K, Ay AS, 'Efficacy of Botulinum Toxin Injection into Posterior Cricoarytenoid Muscles for the Management of Aspiration in Bilateral Adductor Vocal Fold Paralysis: A Case Series', J Voice (2026), doi:10.1016/j.jvoice.2026.07.018 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvoice.2026.07.018) -- all retrieved via PubMed
